recent_posts.title: Why organizational change fails and how daily practice fixes it
recent_posts.summary: Traditional change management frameworks like Kotter's 8 Steps and ADKAR often fail because they address the what, how, and why of change while underestimating human neuropsychology and organizational culture. Key human factors that derail change include psychological ownership, status quo bias, cognitive overload, and change fatigue. Organizational culture operates across three layers: everyday culture, the business operating system, and hidden stories — and most change efforts only target the middle layer. The missing ingredient is deliberate, consistent practice of new behaviors in real work contexts, not better communication campaigns or training sessions. Small behavioral shifts, repeated across every meeting and interaction, are what actually shift culture and make change stick.

recent_posts.title: Why your operating model determines whether AI investments pay off
recent_posts.summary: Many organizations have improved team-level productivity through Agile and DevOps, yet business outcomes remain elusive. Data from industry reports shows only 8% of end-to-end delivery time is spent building software, with the rest consumed by coordination and overhead. The root cause is the operating model: most enterprises still fund and manage digital work as projects rather than products. A Product Operating Model aligns funding, team structure, and measurement around persistent value streams and business outcomes rather than fixed-scope deliverables. AI amplifies this problem — without the right operating model, AI accelerates output of the wrong things. The post outlines three key levers for the shift: persistent funding tied to value streams, stable cross-functional teams with outcome ownership, and KPIs focused on adoption and revenue rather than velocity and ticket throughput.

recent_posts.title: Why industrial AI is stuck in pilot mode and what it will take to scale
recent_posts.summary: Manufacturing and industrial operations are stuck in AI pilot mode despite years of Industry 4.0 promises. Two core challenges block progress: first, the lack of an integrated digital twin — a unified, contextualized data layer across all OT systems — without which AI can only optimize in silos. Second, and harder, is the inability to fully model the physical twin from digital data alone; experienced operator knowledge and physical-world context cannot be inferred from historical data. The authors outline three stages of AI autonomy (assistance, collaboration, autonomy) and argue that most industrial operations are still at stage one. Bridging the IT/OT divide — analogous to but far deeper than the Dev/Ops gap — is a prerequisite for any meaningful AI scale-up in manufacturing.

recent_posts.title: Why Phoenix Project DevOps principles still apply to AI transformation
recent_posts.summary: The Phoenix Project Graphic Novel Volume 3 releases in April 2026, completing Bill Palmer's transformation story. The piece argues that the DevOps principles from the original 2013 novel — the Three Ways (Flow, Feedback, Continuous Learning), Theory of Constraints, and systems thinking — are more relevant than ever as organizations struggle with AI adoption. The same organizational dysfunctions that plagued Parts Unlimited now manifest in failed AI initiatives: siloed experiments disconnected from value streams, lack of feedback loops causing model drift, and ungoverned AI tool deployments. The developer role shift from executor to orchestrator mirrors Bill's journey from firefighter to systems leader. The graphic novel format is praised for making abstract systems thinking visually intuitive, helping technology leaders build the foundational understanding needed to make AI transformations succeed.

recent_posts.title: Mik Kersten's new book on outcome management in the age of AI
recent_posts.summary: Mik Kersten's forthcoming book 'Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI' argues that AI is eliminating knowledge work output as the primary organizational constraint, shifting the bottleneck to organizational structure itself. The book introduces 'Outcome Management' — a systems-level leadership practice replacing centralized governance with cascading accountability. It presents ten mental models and seven organizational shifts (e.g., Functions to Flow, Chaos to Cadence, Managers to Makers) to help organizations transition from output-focused management to outcome-driven operating models suited for AI-native environments.

recent_posts.title: A five-stage framework for assessing your organization's real AI maturity
recent_posts.summary: A framework from the upcoming book 'Hyperadaptive' outlines five stages organizations move through on the path to becoming AI-native: Foundation, Process Optimization, Agents and Automation, Scaling AI, and Hyperadaptive. Most organizations overestimate their progress, claiming Stage 3 or 4 while actually sitting at Stage 1. The post provides diagnostic checklists for each stage and argues that skipping foundational work — governance, psychological safety, AI champions, learning communities — is why nearly 80% of AI initiatives fail. Moderna's 100% GenAI adoption in six months is cited as evidence that deliberate, stage-by-stage capability building outperforms ambitious leaps.

recent_posts.title: Why AI pilots fail to scale and what organizations must fix first
recent_posts.summary: Nearly 80% of AI initiatives fail to scale beyond the pilot stage, and the root cause is rarely technology. Organizations are trying to deploy powerful AI into rigid, Taylorist structures built for a different era. Three structural barriers block scaling: information friction (knowledge workers waste 9+ hours/week searching for answers), decision bottlenecks from approval layers, and functional silos that prevent cross-departmental spread. Successful AI-native companies like Moderna invest in people-first foundations before scaling — identifying AI champions, creating psychological safety, and allocating protected time for AI learning. The core argument is that organizations must rewire their human systems and governance structures before AI pilots can become enterprise-wide capabilities.

recent_posts.title: Where Is Your Organization in the AI Transformation Journey?
recent_posts.summary: A five-stage diagnostic framework for assessing organizational AI readiness, drawn from the upcoming book 'Hyperadaptive.' Each stage covers indicators of current standing, signals of readiness to advance, and red flags that suggest foundational gaps. Stage 1 focuses on governance and pilots; Stage 2 on process optimization; Stage 3 on trusted automation; Stage 4 on scaling and restructuring; Stage 5 on full hyperadaptive realization with AI-powered sensing and continuous adaptation. The key insight, backed by 2025 DORA research, is that AI amplifies existing organizational strengths or weaknesses, making foundational readiness critical before scaling.

recent_posts.title: Building Your Leadership Pipeline: A Practical Framework for Identifying Future Technology Leaders
recent_posts.summary: A practical framework for identifying and developing first-line technology leaders, based on the paper 'A Nose for Elevating Technology Leaders.' It argues that leadership potential reveals itself through human observation rather than AI-driven metrics, and defines five key characteristics: commitment, curiosity, outcome orientation, people leadership, and technology leadership. The framework centers on 'sniff tests'—real-world stretch assignments that expose genuine leadership behaviors—illustrated with concrete examples like an engineer rebuilding their PC to run an LLM, a junior developer improving code review throughput after reading The Phoenix Project, and an IC turning a vague task into a self-sustaining process. Red flags such as cynicism, credit-stealing, and territoriality are also highlighted. The post concludes that leaders are grown through intentional coaching, regular 1:1s, and timely feedback, and that early identification saves far more than remediation later.

recent_posts.title: Why ‘Move Fast and Break Things’ Is Wrong: Lessons from AWS, eBay, and Google on Speed with Safety
recent_posts.summary: The 'move fast and break things' mantra is challenged with evidence from AWS, eBay, Google, Capital One, and BMW. Drawing from a paper by Adrian Cockcroft and colleagues, the post introduces a faster/cheaper/safer triangle framework—analogous to the CAP theorem—showing that organizations must consciously trade off these three dimensions based on business context. The Capital One 2019 breach illustrates how speed without safety investment creates costly disasters, while BMW's OTA and simulation investments show how upfront safety spending accelerates long-term velocity. Practical strategies include tightening feedback loops, using the OODA loop, optimizing flow, and making trade-offs explicit through scenario framing and decentralized decision-making. The core argument: sustainable speed requires prior investment in resilience, observability, automation, and testing.

top_posts.title: “No Vibe Coding While I’m On Call”: What Happens When AI Writes Your Production Code
top_posts.summary: AI code generation without proper guardrails leads to production incidents. Through a fictional narrative of a company experiencing repeated outages from AI-generated code, the article illustrates four critical failure patterns: AI optimizing code without understanding system context, generating tests that pass but don't validate requirements, documenting features that don't exist, and eroding architectural resilience through incremental changes. The solution involves breaking AI tasks into small verifiable chunks, using AI to critique its own work, verifying documentation against actual code, establishing architectural reviews, and building observability from day one.

top_posts.title: The Key Vibe Coding Practices
top_posts.summary: Explores conversational AI-assisted coding practices that prioritize iterative problem-solving over formal prompt engineering. Emphasizes treating AI interactions like casual conversations, letting errors guide corrections through direct feedback, leveraging AI's broad knowledge of tools and libraries, and progressing from vague initial requests to precise specifications through dialogue.

top_posts.title: AI assisted coding democratizes software development for everyone
top_posts.summary: AI-assisted coding is democratizing software development, enabling non-technical professionals like finance VPs, product managers, and former programmers to write production-grade code. This transformation eliminates traditional barriers like complex setup requirements and framework dependencies, allowing people across various roles to build features, automate workflows, and prototype solutions without extensive programming knowledge. The shift represents a fundamental change in who can participate in software creation.

top_posts.title: Software acquisition processes mirror 1944 sabotage tactics
top_posts.summary: Modern software acquisition processes in defense and large organizations mirror tactics from a 1944 CIA sabotage manual: excessive committees, rigid documentation requirements, and process over outcomes. The Department of Defense's Software Acquisition Pathway (SWP) offers an antidote through lightweight requirements, continuous user engagement, iterative delivery, and empowered product owners. Success stories from Navy Forge and the CIA demonstrate that focusing on small wins, embedding users from day one, and measuring outcomes rather than compliance can break the cycle of self-inflicted bureaucratic sabotage.

top_posts.title: Navigating the Ethical Minefield of AI
top_posts.summary: Learn how to navigate the ethical challenges of AI by cultivating a culture of ethical awareness, embracing humility and adaptability, prioritizing transparency and human oversight, and using AI as a tool for introspection. Discover the key takeaways from Mark Schwartz's book on AI ethics and understand the importance of algorithmic transparency in AI systems.
